finding.claim: Address6.href() interpolates optionalPort into the URL without validating that it is a port number. A string that starts with digits and then contains '@', for example '80@evil.example', produces http://[addr]:80@evil.example/. A URL parser reads '[addr]:80' as userinfo and evil.example as the host, so a link or fetch built from the result can be redirected to an attacker-chosen host. This is exploitable only if the caller passes untrusted input as the port. The signature accepts number|string, and the only guard is the TypeScript type, which is not enforced at runtime.
finding.source: Caller-supplied optionalPort string, e.g. a port taken from a query parameter or request field
finding.sink: Return value of href(), a URL string with an attacker-controlled authority

trace.note: href(optionalPort?: number | string) accepts a string
optionalPort = `:${optionalPort}` with no numeric or range check
returned as `http://[${correctForm()}]${optionalPort}/`, so the port text lands in the authority component

finding.guards_checked: No runtime type or range check on the port. The bracketed host comes from correctForm(), which only emits hex digits and ':', so the host part is safe. The link() method HTML-escapes its output but does not call href(). This is a defense-in-depth gap for callers that pass untrusted ports. Confidence is moderate-to-low because exploitation depends on caller misuse.
